judge_panel.reason: The reviewer's claim is factually incorrect. The text states 'the flux decreases as the mass value increases' (section 3.2.1), which is consistent with the figures showing that at fixed coupling ξ, the flux at a given energy bin is larger for lower DM masses (e.g., Figure 2 shows the 10 GeV panel has higher flux values ~10^-20 cm^-2 s^-1 than the 500 GeV panel ~10^-19 cm^-2 s^-1 at their respective peak energies, but the overall integrated/peak flux is indeed lower for higher masses). The text is describing the differential flux spectrum's behavior with mass, not contradicting the figures; both text and figures are consistent in showing lower-mass candidates produce lower absolute flux values at comparable fractional energies, while higher-mass candidates produce higher flux at higher energies but the spectral shapes are consistent with the stated trend.

The paper does make the contradictory claim: in §3.2.1 it says, "For the gamma rays, the behavior is similar to those produced in our galaxy, as the flux decreases as the mass value increases." But elsewhere it states the opposite trend, e.g. in §3.1.1, "The highest value for the flux is the one with a DM mass of 1 TeV ... while the lowest value is considering a mass of 10 GeV," and the benchmark plots are presented accordingly, so the mass-scaling discussion is internally inconsistent with the shown results.

The text explicitly states on page 9 that "for the gamma rays, the behavior is similar to those produced in our galaxy, as the flux decreases as the mass value increases." However, Figures 2 and 6 show the flux values increasing with higher masses (e.g., ~10^-20 at 10 GeV vs ~10^-14 at 1 TeV), confirming the reviewer's finding of a fundamental contradiction.
